title: The AI Engineer’s Guide to Raising VC — Dani Grant (Jam), Chelcie Taylor (Notable)

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 95%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on interpersonal and human-side skills for AI company building—pitching, trust-building, and founder-investor collaboration—making human factors the closest available taxonomy match despite the topic being fundraising rather than product UX. The fundraising playbook is general-purpose and not tied to any specific application vertical. The session explicitly addresses pre-seed and seed stage fundraising. The content is an introductory playbook designed for first-time fundraisers with no prior VC experience. This is a recorded conference presentation from the AI Engineer World's Fair. All evidence anchors are directly quoted from the transcript with grade said_in_transcript.

summary: Dani Grant and Chelcie Taylor deliver a practical, tactics-focused session on raising VC for AI engineers. They open with audience polls debunking myths: revenue and a finished product are not required at pre-seed/seed, and leaving a full-time job signals conviction but is firm-dependent. Dani shares that raising pre-product was easier because everything was potential. The principle 'ask for advice, get money; ask for money, get advice' frames relationship-building. Cold outreach is covered with real funded email examples showing that specificity, engaging with VC content, and compelling rather than selling are key. The session then moves to pitch meetings. Chelcie identifies the top mistakes AI engineers make: overfocusing on technology instead of articulating 'why you, why now,' and not painting a path to a billion-dollar company. She outlines the core questions VCs ask: product vision and velocity, ICP, revenue and monetization hypotheses, and team-building ability. Good answers to competitor questions acknowledge competitors, map them on axes, and differentiate with a unique insight. For go-to-market, founders should offer directional frameworks (e.g., PLG) and pricing hypotheses while signaling openness to experiment. For team, founders should highlight their ability to attract top AI engineers. Design partners or customer interviews serve as evidence even without a product. Pitch meetings should be bidirectional — the best founders ask VCs why they passed on or liked competitors. Chelcie advises not using the meeting to go deep on technology unless meeting a technical investor; many firms hold a separate technical deep-dive. Founders should also use meetings to test whether they want to work with the VC. When wrapping up, founders should proactively ask about next steps and the VC's process, then send a polished pitch deck immediately after — not during — since the deck is a brochure for the VC's teammates, not the person in the room. Dani references Jam's original 2020 pitch deck at deck.jam.dev as an example. Chelcie closes by noting that everything in the meeting equips the VC to sell you internally, and shares her email (ctaylor@notablecap.com) for cold outreach.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: When to Raise VC and What You Need
sections.summary: Interactive audience polls establish that revenue, a product, and full-time commitment are not strictly required for pre-seed/seed raises. Investors back founders, teams, and vision. Leaving a job signals conviction but is firm-dependent. Dani shares that raising pre-product was easier than after building.

sections.title: Cold Email Outreach and Real Examples
sections.summary: Chelcie confirms she reads cold emails, especially those triggered by warm signals like engaging with her content. Multiple real cold emails are shown that led to investments. Key principle: be compelling, not selling — the email's job is to get a response, with hyper-specific asks and brevity emphasized.

sections.title: Pitch Meetings: Why You, Why Now, and the Path to Scale
sections.summary: The session covers what happens in pitch meetings. Chelcie's top mistakes for engineers: overfocusing on technology instead of 'why you, why now,' and not painting the path to a billion-dollar company. Good answers ground pitches in a core problem and demonstrate unique insights from lived experience. Design partners or customer interviews anchor potential. Meetings should be bidirectional — one founder impressed an investment committee by declining to make up an answer. Chelcie advises practicing with less ideal funds first.

sections.title: Core VC Questions: Product, ICP, Revenue, and Team
sections.summary: Chelcie outlines the remaining core pitch questions: product vision and velocity, ideal customer profile (ICP), revenue and monetization hypotheses, and team-building ability. Founders should come with directional thinking and frameworks even without exact answers, signal awareness of monetization models, and highlight their network to attract top AI engineers.

sections.title: Good Answers: Competitors and Go-to-Market
sections.summary: Chelcie and Dani detail what good answers sound like. For competitors: acknowledge they exist, map them on axes, and differentiate with a unique insight — hiding competitors makes you untrustworthy since VCs have likely met them all. Clay is cited as an example. For go-to-market: offer directional frameworks (e.g., PLG) and pricing hypotheses while signaling openness to experiment, and ask VCs for feedback.

sections.title: Ending Meetings, Follow-Up Materials, and Closing
sections.summary: Founders should proactively ask about next steps and the VC's process at meeting end. Send the pitch deck after the meeting — not during — since it is a brochure for the VC's teammates who weren't in the room. Dani references Jam's 2020 deck at deck.jam.dev. Chelcie notes everything in the meeting equips the VC to sell you internally, and shares her email for cold outreach.

demonstrations: Multiple real cold email examples shown that led to actual VC investments, ranging from specific meeting follow-ups to terse content-engagement messages
Audience polls conducted on whether revenue, product, full-time commitment, and co-founders are needed to raise VC
Example of a founder at investment committee who said he could make up an answer but wanted to be thoughtful, impressing the team
Jam's original 2020 pitch deck referenced as a public example at deck.jam.dev
Clay cited as a competitor-answer example: acknowledging ZoomInfo exists but differentiating by aggregating the most data sources
limitations: Much of the advice is firm and partner dependent, particularly around full-time commitment requirements
The session focuses on pre-seed and seed stages; later-stage funds have different expectations like ARR growth
Technical deep-dive practices vary by firm — some VCs are highly technical and may want tech detail in the first meeting
quantitativeClaims: Jam is used by 65,000+ developers (from description, not transcript)
Notable Capital has $5B AUM (from description, not transcript)
Chelcie posts LinkedIn content two to three times per week as a signal to entrepreneurs
